questions.question: Agriculture earns only 2–3 per cent of GDP. Give the levers that show it remains vital to South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: It feeds more than sixty million people; it employs around five per cent of the formal workforce plus a large seasonal and informal workforce concentrated in rural districts with few alternatives; it supplies the agro-processing industry (mills, refineries, canneries, cellars, abattoirs), so the whole value chain far outweighs the farm-gate percentage; it earns export income through citrus, wine, grapes, wool, macadamias and surplus maize; and it anchors rural settlement, slowing depopulation and keeping small towns alive.

questions.question: Describe the location of the Maize Triangle and explain the factors favouring and hindering maize production there.
questions.expected_answer: The triangle sweeps across the interior plateau — the Free State (largest producer), North West around Lichtenburg, and the Mpumalanga highveld around Ermelo. Favouring: summer rainfall of roughly 500–800 mm in the growing season, long hot frost-free summers, deep fertile well-drained soils on gently rolling land suited to machinery, and the standing support web of silos, railways, mills, futures pricing and cultivar research. Hindering: rainfall variability and recurring drought (thunderstorm rain that some seasons fails), hail and early frost, erosion-prone soils, rising diesel, fertiliser and seed costs, and climate change shifting rainfall patterns.

questions.question: Define food security, state South Africa's national-versus-household paradox, and give two strategies aimed at it.
questions.expected_answer: Food security exists when all people, at all times, have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food for an active healthy life. The paradox: South Africa is food secure at national level — it grows enough staples or imports shortfalls — yet millions of households are food insecure because unemployment and poverty block economic access. Strategies: access-side measures such as the National School Nutrition Programme (about nine million learners) and social grants, plus support for small-scale farmers, food gardens, reduced post-harvest losses and drought-tolerant cultivars.
